card.official_title: PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Limit new tax exemptions from the spending cap and require special-tax audits
card.yes_means: A yes vote would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenues from the state spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes.
card.no_means: A no vote would keep current spending-limit rules and existing audit practices without adding these requirements.

what_changes.today: The State Auditor conducts some one-time audits, but not under this proposed requirement for special-tax initiatives.
what_changes.if_passes: Audits would begin at 25 percent of required signatures, identify ways to cut program costs by 10 percent, and be summarized in the voter guide if the initiative qualifies.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Some State Auditor reviews already happen regularly.
what_changes.if_passes: Programs funded by special taxes created or increased after January 1, 2026, would be audited every four years, using new tax revenues to pay audit costs.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The state has a constitutional tax-spending limit, with exclusions for spending such as infrastructure.
what_changes.if_passes: The state might no longer be able to exclude new special-tax spending from that limit.
what_changes.label: prediction

who_is_affected: People who use programs funded by new or increased special taxes
Taxpayers and voters considering special-tax initiatives

fiscal_impact.text: The net fiscal effect is unknown. Audit costs likely would be in the low millions of dollars per year and grow over time. New special-tax revenues would pay one-time and ongoing audit costs for taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. The General Fund would cover one-time audits for proposed special taxes that never reach the ballot or are rejected by voters. Longer voter guides would cost a few hundred thousand dollars per qualifying initiative. Effective audit recommendations could produce savings.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

steelman_yes.headline: Supporters argue regular independent audits would make tax-funded programs more effective and improve the services people receive.
more_reasons: Supporters argue public audit summaries would help voters judge whether programs need more money before approving special taxes.
Supporters argue applying the spending limit to new taxes would better protect taxpayers.

best_evidence.text: The measure requires audits every four years, including recommendations to improve program efficiency.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Savings or better services could result if policymakers adopt audit recommendations and those recommendations work.
best_evidence.label: prediction

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters say taxpayers and people relying on education, health care, and other public services would benefit.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters respond that funding alone does not ensure good services: reducing waste and improving programs can help the people who depend on them.

steelman_no.headline: Opponents argue the tax restrictions risk blocking the proposed billionaire tax, threatening funding that keeps hospitals open and health care affordable.
more_reasons: Opponents argue losing that proposed revenue would also threaten support for public education and food assistance.
Opponents argue the new audit requirements would cost the state time and money.

best_evidence.text: Under Proposition 41, another voter-approved measure on the same ballot is void only if it conflicts with Proposition 41 and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Opponents predict Proposition 41 would prevent the proposed billionaire tax from providing money to keep hospitals open and health care affordable.
best_evidence.label: prediction
best_evidence.whose: Opponents in the official ballot argument

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents say rejecting the measure would protect working families and people who rely on publicly funded health care and other services.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Opponents respond that audit benefits do not outweigh the risk of losing proposed service funding, especially when the audits themselves add costs.

crux.text: The dispute is whether added oversight and tighter spending rules would improve public services enough to justify their costs and limits on new revenue. Opponents emphasize risks to the proposed billionaire tax; supporters emphasize better results from each tax dollar.

evidence.text: The official summary makes cancellation of another ballot measure conditional: it must conflict with Proposition 41, and Proposition 41 must receive more affirmative votes.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst says the state might not be able to exclude new special-tax spending from the limit; the analysis does not establish that Proposition 40 would automatically be canceled.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The 10 percent figure is a requirement to identify possible annual cost reductions in pre-election audits, not a requirement to carry out those cuts.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The General Fund would pay for audits of proposed special taxes that never reach the ballot or are rejected by voters.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Savings depend on future policy decisions and whether audit recommendations prove effective; their size is unknown.
evidence.label: prediction

turing_yes.reason: The card captures supporters’ central merits case: public audits could improve accountability, program efficiency, and services, while helping voters assess proposed taxes. It could more explicitly reflect their argument that the spending-limit rule protects taxpayers, but it gives that argument in the additional reasons.

turing_no.reason: The card captures opponents’ strongest merits claim in the official argument: the measure could impede the proposed billionaire tax and put funding for health care and other services at risk, with audits also costing money and time. The wording should preserve the source’s conditions and uncertainty rather than making the tax consequence sound settled.

swap_notes: Both headlines use parallel 'Supporters/Opponents argue' framing, but the No headline’s 'would block' is more definite and forceful than the Yes headline’s 'would make ... more effective.' Keep the No argument, but make its conditional nature clear.
fidelity_problems: The fiscal-impact text omits a material exception: the analysis says the General Fund would pay one-time audit costs for special-tax initiatives that do not reach the ballot or are rejected by voters. Add this alongside the statement that costs for taxes approved by voters or the Legislature are paid from new tax revenues.

The No best-evidence claim says conflicting measures are void if Prop. 41 receives more affirmative votes, but omits the other required condition: the measures must conflict. The card’s separate evidence point states this correctly; make the best-evidence claim equally complete.

The No headline says the restrictions 'would block' the proposed billionaire tax. The official opposing argument makes that claim, but the analysis says only that the state might not be able to exclude new special-tax spending from the limit, and the summary makes voiding another measure conditional on conflict and Prop. 41 receiving more affirmative votes. Phrase the headline as an opponents’ prediction or risk, not a settled result.
loaded_or_overconfident: “Would block” in the No headline sounds certain despite the source’s conditional ballot-conflict rule and the Legislative Analyst’s more qualified description of the spending-limit effect.
verdict.instructions: 1. In the fiscal-impact text, add that General Fund funds would cover one-time audits for proposed special taxes that never reach the ballot or are rejected; distinguish these from audit costs for taxes approved by voters or the Legislature, which are paid from new revenues. 2. In the No best-evidence claim, state that another measure is void only if it conflicts with Prop. 41 and Prop. 41 receives more affirmative votes. 3. Revise the No headline so it presents blocking the proposed billionaire tax as opponents’ claimed risk, rather than a certain outcome.

turing_yes.reason: The card captures supporters’ central merits case: independent audits and public summaries could improve accountability, inform tax decisions, and make tax-funded services work better. The spending-limit point is also a fair statement of the supporters’ taxpayer-protection argument.

turing_no.reason: The card fairly presents opponents’ principal merits concern: the measure could constrain the proposed billionaire tax and put service funding at risk, while adding audit costs. It appropriately presents this as opponents’ argument rather than an established outcome, and includes the ballot measure’s conditional-conflict rule.

swap_notes: The headline structure and attribution are parallel. The No headline is more specific about the threatened services, reflecting the opponents’ central argument in the source; the Yes headline’s “would make” is somewhat more certain than the No headline’s “risk.”
loaded_or_overconfident: Yes headline: “would make tax-funded programs more effective” is more certain than the analysis, which says savings or improved services could result if policymakers implement recommendations and they prove effective. Consider “could help make” instead.
